title: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate
subtitle: ESR for detection of acute and chronic inflammation
summary: ESR measurement for assessment of systemic inflammation, infection, and autoimmune disease.
introduction: The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) measures the rate at which red blood cells settle in plasma over 1 hour. It is an indirect measure of inflammation, correlating with acute-phase protein synthesis. ESR is non-specific but useful for detecting systemic inflammation and monitoring disease activity.

rows.name: ESR
rows.referenceRange: Adult female <20; Male <15 (age-adjusted: female (age+10)/2, male age/2)
lowInterpretation: ESR <10 mm/h: normal. In absence of symptoms, inflammation unlikely.
Very low ESR (<1 mm/h): unusual; seen in polycythaemia, spherocytosis, hypofibrinogenaemia.
highInterpretation: ESR 20–40 mm/h: mild elevation. Suggests inflammation, infection, or malignancy; wide differential.
ESR 40–100 mm/h: moderate-to-significant elevation. Usually indicates acute infection, acute inflammatory disease, or malignancy.
ESR >100 mm/h: marked elevation. Suggests severe infection (endocarditis, TB), malignancy, or vasculitis.
notes: Non-specific: elevated in infection, autoimmune disease, malignancy, age, anaemia, renal failure, hyperglobulinaemia, pregnancy.
Rises more slowly than CRP in acute infection (peaks at 24–48 hours); useful for monitoring chronic disease.
Anaemia increases ESR artificially (RBCs settle faster); low Hb may elevate ESR despite minimal inflammation.
Age-adjusted normal ranges critical in older patients; normal may be 20–30 mm/h in elderly.

urgentFindings: ESR >100 mm/h: significant inflammation; investigate for endocarditis, TB, vasculitis, or malignancy.
ESR 20–40 mm/h + fever + localising symptoms: supports diagnosis of infection; proceed with imaging/cultures.
Markedly elevated ESR (>80) + anaemia (Hb <100): anaemia contributing to ESR elevation; assess response to anaemia treatment.
overrides: Do not use ESR as sole marker of inflammation or infection; always correlate with CRP and clinical findings.
ESR may be normal early in acute infection (first 24 hours); repeat if clinically indicated.
High ESR with negative structural investigations requires investigation for occult infection, malignancy, or autoimmune disease.

commonPatterns.title: Acute bacterial infection
interpretation: ESR lags CRP in acute infection
actions: Obtain blood cultures and source investigation
Monitor CRP response to therapy (better short-term marker)

commonPatterns.title: Unexplained elevated ESR (malignancy screening)
interpretation: Elevated ESR in absence of infection suggests malignancy
Anaemia may contribute to ESR elevation

rationale: CRP rises faster in acute infection; informs timing of infection
ESR elevated with normal CRP/infection workup
